subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Weave a Rule, Read a Rule

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us make paper mats, p.92
tasks_in_class.description: Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips in alternating 1-under-1-over / 1-over-1-under pattern to make a mat.
Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven by studying the first two rows and writing the pattern rule.
Work out the steps for either of the two shown weave designs; write the pattern for each row until it starts repeating.
Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper; complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.

time_bands.activity: Students fold a sheet, cut slits, and weave colour strips following the alternating rule — Let us make paper mats, p.92 ("fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips...."). Pairs compare finished mats and say aloud what the row rule is.

Class examines the printed 2-over-1-under mat image and individually writes the row rule — Q2, p.93 ("figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven...."). Two or three students share their written rule; the class refines the wording together.

Students choose one of the two weave designs in Q4, p.93 ("work out the steps for either of the two shown weave designs....") and write row rules until the pattern repeats. Sharing reveals that both designs eventually repeat.

Students transfer the given weave rule to grid paper — Let Us Try, p.93 ("draw the given weave pattern on grid paper....") — completing as much of the grid as time allows and marking where the repeat begins.

periods.teacher_notes: T-3 (weaving with the 4-row rule) is closely parallel in structure to T-1; it is noted here as additional hands-on practice and can be set if pairs finish the mat quickly. A common error is reversing the rule on even-numbered rows — remind students to re-read the rule before beginning each new row rather than relying on memory.
materials: Plain paper sheets for mat base

tasks_in_class.description: Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap; count how many fit together.
Try fitting square cutouts around a point without any gap or overlap; count how many squares are needed.
Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point; count how many fit together without gaps or overlaps.
Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern; continue the pattern on the grid and colour it appropriately.

time_bands.activity: Groups receive triangle cutouts and fit them around a shared point on paper — Find Out, p.94 ("fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap...."). Each group records how many fit.

Groups swap to square cutouts and repeat — Find Out, p.94 ("try fitting square cutouts around a point without any gap or overlap...."). They then reason whether a fifth square could fit — Find Out, p.94 ("can 5 squares fit together around a point....?") — and write one sentence explaining why or why not.

Groups try hexagon cutouts at a point — Find Out, p.94 ("try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point....") — and record results. A brief whole-class comparison of all three results is shared: triangles, squares, and hexagons all tile; pentagons and octagons (previewed) do not.

Each student identifies the two shapes in the book's mixed tessellation and continues the pattern on dot paper — Find Out, p.95 ("identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern; continue the pattern...."). Students colour the two shape families differently to make the rule visible.

periods.teacher_notes: T-11 (octagon drawing check) and T-12, T-13, T-14 (octagon+square and square+triangle tilings) address more complex multi-shape patterns; note these as additional practice — T-12 and T-13 are particularly rich for reasoning about which shapes meet at a vertex. A common error is students placing shapes with slight overlaps and declaring they tessellate; ask them to slide one cutout away and check whether the gap is truly zero.
materials: Pre-cut regular triangle, square, hexagon, octagon, and pentagon card cutouts (one set per group)

tasks_in_class.description: Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify the geometrical shapes created.
How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces? Observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?
Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle) from the rhombus pieces?
Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal (scalene) from the rhombus pieces?
How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make by fitting 2 rhombus triangles? Explore the possibilities.

time_bands.activity: Students cut a rhombus along both diagonals to get four triangular pieces, then fit two together and trace the resulting shape — Try This, p.97 ("cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify...."). Pairs share what shapes they found.

Students measure the sides of the triangle types they can make with two pieces — Try This Q1, p.97 ("observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?"). They then reason whether an equilateral triangle — Try This Q2, p.97 — or a scalene triangle — Try This Q3, p.97 — is achievable and write a one-sentence justification for each.

Students fit two rhombus triangles to find all the distinct 4-sided shapes they can make — Try This Q4, p.98 ("how many different 4-sided shapes can you make....?"). Each shape is traced and its sides labelled equal or unequal.

Quick class share: students name the shapes they found (parallelogram, kite, rectangle) and say in one word what makes each different from the others — equal opposite sides, equal adjacent sides, right angles.

periods.teacher_notes: T-19 (paper-folding the equilateral triangle to check angles) and T-21 (measuring quadrilateral sides) extend the side-comparison work and can be assigned as additional practice if time permits. A common error is assuming that two rhombus triangles always make the same parallelogram — ask students to try flipping one piece before joining.

periods.activity_title: Four Pieces, Many Shapes — and Meeting the Kite

tasks_in_class.description: Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given.
Use 3 rhombus triangles to form shapes; count sides of each; try creating a 3-sided, 4-sided, and 5-sided shape.
Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) can be made.
Match 7 property statements to the correct shape from: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram. Note shapes that match more than one statement.
Make a kite by paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward); observe what shapes appear inside the kite.

time_bands.activity: Students open to the grid in Try This Q6, p.99 ("draw two different kites and two different parallelograms....") and draw each shape, using their traced pieces from the earlier exploration as a reference for what makes each type distinct.

Students use 3 rhombus triangles — Try This Q7, p.99 ("use 3 rhombus triangles to form shapes....") — to find a 3-sided, 4-sided, and 5-sided shape, tracing each. They then use all 4 pieces — Try This Q8, p.99 ("use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes can be made....") — and work through the list, ticking shapes they achieve.

Students read the seven property statements in Which Shape Am I?, p.100 ("match 7 property statements to the correct shape....") and write the matching shape name beside each. The class discusses any statement that fits more than one shape.

Students fold a square sheet to make a kite — Kites, p.100 ("make a kite by paper-folding from a square....") — and observe the shapes visible inside it. They label the two pairs of equal adjacent sides on their folded kite.

periods.teacher_notes: T-25 (tangram activity) explores the same quadrilateral properties through a different manipulative and can be noted as rich optional extension. A common error in the property-matching task is assigning 'all sides equal' only to the square — guide students to check the rhombus definition carefully.
materials: Rhombus triangle pieces from the previous exploration (or freshly cut)
Square paper sheets for kite folding

section_titles: Play with Circles and Circle Designs

tasks_in_class.description: Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed; try with different diameter pairs.
Join numbered circle points (1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, ...) to make a string-art design; think of a way to make the overlapping-circles image.

time_bands.activity: Students use a compass and ruler to draw a circle, mark two diameters, and join the four endpoints — Play with Circles, p.101 ("draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints...."). They measure the four angles of the resulting shape with a protractor or folding, then repeat with a different pair of diameters and compare results.

Students follow the numbered skip-rule to draw chords connecting the points on the circumference — Circle Designs, p.101 ("join numbered circle points (1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12...) to make a string-art design...."). After completing the design, they look at the overlapping-circles image and discuss in pairs how they might construct it.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who finish the skip-rule design quickly can be encouraged to invent their own skip number and predict the shape before drawing it. A common error in the diameter task is joining non-adjacent endpoints diagonally rather than following the order around the circle — ask students to label the four points A, B, C, D before joining.
materials: Plain white paper (2 sheets per student)
Pre-printed circle with 12 numbered points (one per student)

periods.activity_title: Cube Nets, Missing Cubes, and the Painted Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net.
Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c).
Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces.
Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle) in a line.

time_bands.activity: Students study the three face-pattern views of a cube and draw each pattern in its correct net position — Cube Connections Q1, p.102 ("given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position...."). Pairs compare their nets and justify their face placements.

Students count the small unit cubes that have been removed from each of the three frame pictures — Cube Connections Q2, p.102 ("work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c)...."). They write a number sentence showing total cubes minus remaining cubes for each frame.

Students work through the painted-cube puzzle — Cube Connections Q3, p.102 ("Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red....") — by thinking about corner, edge, face-centre, and interior positions systematically. They record how many small cubes fall into each category.

Students apply the five clues one at a time to place Tanu's seven shapes in order — Puzzle, p.102 ("use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes in a line....") — crossing off possibilities as each clue is applied.

periods.teacher_notes: The painted-cube problem is the most demanding task in this unit; students who struggle should be encouraged to build or sketch a 3×3×3 grid and physically mark corner, edge, and face positions. A common error is confusing 'face-centre' cubes (one painted face) with 'edge' cubes (two painted faces) — ask students to count how many faces of each small cube touch the outside surface.
materials: Unit cube blocks or small blocks (optional, for the painted-cube visualisation)
Printed net diagram from textbook p.102 (or students copy from book)

tasks_in_class.description: Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models; observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.

time_bands.activity: Students cut out the nets from the back of the book, score the fold lines, and fold and glue each solid — Icosahedron and Dodecahedron, p.103 ("use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models...."). Pairs help each other hold faces while glue sets.

Students examine their finished models: they name the face shape of each solid, count how many faces meet at a single vertex, and count the total number of edges by running a finger along each one and making a tally — Icosahedron and Dodecahedron, p.103 ("observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.").

Whole-class comparison: pairs share their counts for faces, edges-per-vertex, and total edges for both solids. The class records the results in a two-column table (icosahedron vs dodecahedron) and notices similarities and differences with the cube's known counts.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who built cubes and examined their nets in the previous cube connections unit bring useful vocabulary — face, edge, vertex — that transfers directly to this comparison. A common error is miscounting edges by counting each edge twice (once per adjacent face); encourage students to mark each edge with a pencil dot as they count so no edge is tallied twice.
materials: Nets from the back of the textbook (pre-cut or cut during the unit)
Tally chart template or plain paper for recording

items.prompt: A mat is woven with this rule: Row 1 — 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under. Row 2 — 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over. Write the rule for Row 3 and Row 4.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 3 is the same as Row 1: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under. Row 4 is the same as Row 2: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over. The pattern repeats every 2 rows.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the repeating unit in the alternating over-under rule and continue it.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can colour a paper strip and physically fold it over and under to feel the rule; fast finishers can write the rule for a 2-over-1-under mat.

exercise.book_ref: Let us make paper mats, p.92
exercise.description: Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips in alternating 1-under-1-over / 1-over-1-under pattern to make a mat.

items.prompt: Mina places regular triangle tiles around a single point so there are no gaps and no overlaps. How many triangles does she use?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 equilateral triangles fit exactly around a point with no gaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fit triangle cutouts around a single point and count until the full rotation is complete with no gap.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses triangles with squares — 4 squares fit around a point, not 4 triangles.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Possible guess from pentagon context; 5 triangles leave a visible gap around the point.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Over-counts, perhaps confusing the number of triangle sides with the number of tiles.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can cut and physically place triangle pieces around a dot on paper; fast finishers can check whether the same result holds for a point in the interior of a triangle tiling.

exercise.description: Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap; count how many fit together.

items.prompt: Ravi places regular hexagon tiles snugly around one point. How many hexagons meet at that point?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 regular hexagons fit exactly around a point with no gaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place hexagon cutouts around a single point until the full rotation is covered without overlap.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Only 2 hexagons would leave a large gap; likely a guess without testing.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses hexagons with squares — 4 squares fit around a point.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the number of sides of a hexagon (6) with the count of tiles around a point.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use hexagon cutouts and a dot on paper; fast finishers can draw and shade a honeycomb patch showing three hexagons around every interior vertex.

exercise.description: Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point; count how many fit together without gaps or overlaps.

items.prompt: Priya cuts a rhombus along both diagonals and gets 4 triangular pieces. She fits 2 pieces together along a long side. Name one shape she could make and describe what it looks like.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One shape she could make is a larger isosceles triangle (two equal sides and one longer base), or a parallelogram with two pairs of equal opposite sides. Any one correct shape with an accurate description is acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Physically join two rhombus triangle pieces along matching sides and trace the resulting outline.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can cut and join actual pieces before writing; fast finishers can name a second distinct shape and explain how they positioned the pieces differently.

exercise.description: Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify the geometrical shapes created.

items.prompt: Arjun uses all 4 rhombus triangular pieces. He tries to make a rectangle. Can he do it? Write yes or no and give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, a rectangle can be made by arranging all 4 pieces so that a longer rhombus piece forms each end and the four right-angle corners align to form four right angles. (Accept any correct arrangement with a valid reason.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange all four triangular pieces to align right-angle corners and check that opposite sides are equal and all corners are right angles.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use actual cut pieces and try all orientations; fast finishers can list a second named shape from the list (pentagon, hexagon, octagon) that they can or cannot make and explain why.

exercise.description: Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) can be made.

items.prompt: Seema folds a square sheet along its diagonal, then folds corner A and corner B inward to make a kite. Which of the following is true about the kite she makes?

options.label: A
options.text: All four sides of the kite are equal.

options.label: B
options.text: The kite has no equal sides at all.

options.label: C
options.text: The kite has two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other.

options.label: D
options.text: The kite has two pairs of equal sides that are opposite each other.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The kite has two pairs of equal adjacent (next-to-each-other) sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify which sides were formed by the same fold and note that they share a vertex, making them adjacent.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses a kite with a rhombus — a rhombus has all four sides equal, but kite folds produce two different side lengths.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses kite with parallelogram — equal opposite sides define a parallelogram, not a kite.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Ignores the symmetry of the fold — the fold creates two pairs of equal sides by construction.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can re-fold the square and measure the sides with a ruler; fast finishers can draw a kite on grid paper and mark which sides are equal with tick marks.

exercise.description: Make a kite by paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward); observe what shapes appear inside the kite.

items.section_title: Play with Circles and Circle Designs
items.prompt: Draw a circle. Mark its centre. Draw two diameters that are not the same. Join the four endpoints in order. What shape do you get? Write its name and one thing you notice about its sides or angles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Joining the four endpoints of two diameters always gives a rectangle (or a special rectangle — a square — if the diameters are perpendicular). All four angles are right angles; opposite sides are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw two diameters and join their four endpoints; check that opposite sides span equal chords and that corners are right angles.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use a compass and trace the endpoints before drawing; fast finishers can try two more pairs of diameters and check whether the result is always a rectangle.

exercise.description: Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed; try with different diameter pairs.

items.prompt: Renu builds an icosahedron from its net. What shape are all its faces?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All 20 faces of an icosahedron are equilateral triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Examine the net and the finished model — each face is a triangle, and there are 20 of them.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the icosahedron with a cube — a cube has square faces.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the icosahedron with a dodecahedron — a dodecahedron has pentagonal faces.
what_each_option_reveals.A: May be associating the hexagonal pattern in tessellation work with 3D solids — hexagons do not appear as faces here.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can look at or hold their built model and count face sides; fast finishers can compare the face counts of icosahedron and dodecahedron and record them in a table.

exercise.description: Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models; observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.

items.prompt: A mat is woven with the rule: 2 over, 1 under. Ravi says Row 3 will be exactly the same as Row 1. Is he right? Write yes or no and explain why in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Row 3 is the same as Row 1. In a 2-over-1-under pattern the rule repeats every 3 rows (or shifts by one, depending on the variant), so Row 3 matches Row 1 in structure.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write out the rule for Row 1, Row 2, Row 3 and check whether Row 3 matches Row 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can draw a small grid and shade the over and under positions row by row; fast finishers can write the rule for a 2-over-2-under mat and state when it first repeats.

exercise.description: Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven by studying the first two rows and writing the pattern rule.

items.prompt: Four squares fit perfectly around a point. Can a fifth square also fit at the same point without any gap or overlap? Write yes or no and give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. Four squares already fill the complete turn around the point with no space left, so a fifth square cannot fit without overlapping one of the others.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that four squares already cover the full rotation around a point, leaving no room for a fifth.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can place four square tiles around a point and physically try to insert a fifth; fast finishers can calculate the corner angle of a square and explain using total degrees around a point.

exercise.description: Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?

items.prompt: Look at the grid below. Two shapes make the tessellating pattern. Name both shapes. Then write one sentence about how they fit together without gaps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two shapes are equilateral triangles and squares. They fit together without gaps because the angles at each meeting point add up to a full turn — the triangles fill the corners left between the squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify each shape by counting its sides, then explain that their angles combine to fill the space around every meeting point.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can refer to the textbook grid and trace the outline of one of each shape; fast finishers can continue the pattern for two more rows on dot paper.

exercise.description: Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern; continue the pattern on the grid and colour it appropriately.

items.prompt: Laila joins two rhombus triangular pieces. She measures the sides of the triangle she makes and finds two sides equal and one side different. What type of triangle is this?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Isosceles triangle — it has exactly two equal sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the measured side counts (two equal, one different) to the definition of an isosceles triangle.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Equilateral requires all three sides equal — the student has not yet checked the third side or has confused the term.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Scalene requires all three sides different — contradicts the measured result of two equal sides.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Right-angled describes an angle property, not side lengths; the student may be confusing two classification systems.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can mark equal sides with tick marks before choosing; fast finishers can sketch all three triangle types and label their equal sides.

exercise.description: How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces? Observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?

items.prompt: Meena has 4 rhombus triangular pieces. She says she can make an equilateral triangle — one where all three sides are equal — using exactly 2 pieces. Is she correct? Write yes or no and explain your answer in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. When two rhombus triangles are joined, one pair of sides matches but the third side of the new triangle is longer than the other two, so an equilateral triangle cannot be made this way.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Join two pieces and measure all three sides of the resulting triangle to check whether they are equal.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can join pieces and measure sides with a ruler before deciding; fast finishers can explore whether any combination of the four pieces ever gives an equilateral triangle.

exercise.description: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle) from the rhombus pieces?

items.prompt: Which shape has all four sides equal AND all four angles are right angles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Square — it is the only quadrilateral with all four sides equal and all four angles as right angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each shape's properties against both conditions: equal sides AND right angles — only the square satisfies both.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Rectangle has right angles but opposite (not all four) sides equal, so it fails the equal-sides condition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Rhombus has all sides equal but its angles are generally not right angles, so it fails the right-angle condition.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Parallelogram has equal opposite sides and equal opposite angles but neither condition is fully met here.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can draw each shape and tick boxes for 'all sides equal' and 'all right angles'; fast finishers can write a statement that distinguishes a square from a rhombus using only one property.

exercise.description: Match 7 property statements to the correct shape from: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram. Note shapes that match more than one statement.

items.prompt: Refer to the net of a cube in your book (Cube Connections Q1, p.102). One face shows a star, the opposite face shows a dot. On the net, the star is on the top square. Where should the dot be drawn? Write the position (for example: bottom square, or the square directly below the star) and give one reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The dot should be placed on the face that will fold to be directly opposite the star. In a standard cross-shaped net, the face opposite the top square is the one three squares away along the central column (the bottom square of the column). Reason: opposite faces of a cube are never adjacent on the net — they are separated by one face in between.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the fold of each face on the net mentally and identify which face ends up directly opposite the star face when the net is folded.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can cut and fold the net to physically check the opposite face; fast finishers can mark all three opposite-face pairs on the net.

exercise.description: Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net.

items.prompt: Tanu places 7 shapes in a line using these clues: the circle is in the middle; both squares are next to each other; the hexagon is at one end. Write the order of all 7 shapes from left to right. (The shapes are: 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid order satisfying the stated clues: hexagon, triangle, square, square, circle, triangle, rectangle (or its mirror). The circle occupies position 4 (middle of 7), the two squares are adjacent, and the hexagon is at position 1. Other valid arrangements satisfying all five original clues in the book are also acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the circle in position 4, put the hexagon at either end, then fit the two squares together in the remaining spaces while satisfying any remaining clues.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can write each shape on a slip of paper and physically move them; fast finishers can find a second different valid arrangement and state which clue allows two solutions.

exercise.description: Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle) in a line.

items.prompt: A weave pattern on grid paper starts: Row 1 — shade, blank, shade, blank. Row 2 — blank, shade, blank, shade. What does Row 3 look like?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 3 repeats Row 1: shade, blank, shade, blank.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the 2-row repeating unit and apply it to Row 3.

what_each_option_reveals.B: This is Row 2 — the student has continued the alternation incorrectly, adding one extra shift.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Groups the shaded squares together — confuses the 1-over-1-under alternation with a 2-over-2-under rule.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reverses the grouping — same confusion as B but in the opposite order.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can copy the first two rows on grid paper and colour them, then continue; fast finishers can draw Row 4 and Row 5 and explain the repeating unit in their own words.

exercise.description: Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper; complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw one kite. Mark the two pairs of equal sides with tick marks to show which sides are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A valid kite drawn on the grid with two pairs of adjacent equal sides, each pair marked with a single tick. The two pairs must be adjacent (sharing a vertex), not opposite.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a quadrilateral where one diagonal is a line of symmetry; mark the two sides on each side of that diagonal as equal.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can fold a square paper to make the kite shape and then trace it onto the grid; fast finishers can draw a second kite with different proportions and mark its equal sides.

exercise.description: Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given.

items.prompt: A solid 3×3×3 cube is made of small unit cubes. A tunnel of 1 unit is drilled straight through the middle from front to back, removing those small cubes. How many small cubes are removed?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 small cubes are removed. The tunnel goes through the centre column from front face to back face, removing 1 small cube from each of the 3 layers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the small cubes in a straight 1-unit-wide column running through all 3 layers of the 3×3×3 cube.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can stack 3 unit blocks in a line and count them; fast finishers can calculate how many remain after the tunnel and compare to Q2 in the book.

exercise.description: Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c).

items.prompt: Nisha makes a 3×3×3 cube from 27 small cubes and paints all the outside faces red. How many small cubes have paint on exactly 2 faces?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12 small cubes have exactly 2 painted faces. These are the edge cubes — the cubes that sit along an edge of the big cube but are not at a corner. A 3×3×3 cube has 12 edges, and each edge has exactly 1 such middle cube (not at a corner), giving 12 × 1 = 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the edge-position cubes (not at corners) — each lies on exactly 2 outer faces — and count 1 per edge × 12 edges = 12.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can draw a 3×3 grid for each layer and shade the edge-but-not-corner squares; fast finishers can verify the total by checking that 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27.

exercise.description: Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces.
